newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Thousands protest in Serbia defying Balkan cold.
newsitem.headline: Thousands protest in Serbia defying Balkan cold.

text.p: Thousands of demonstrators against President Slobodan Milosevic ignored the onset of the harsh Balkan winter to march along the streets of Serbia on Sunday demanding their victory at local elections be restored.
Up to 40,000 Belgrade students marched for the 35th day to the cheers of bystanders and now customary flickering lights from flats along their route.

Some 80,000 opposition supporters packed a central square in the bitter cold sending a stark message to the authorities -- bad weather, random arrests or threats by pro-Milosevic demonstrations will not silence their demand for democracy.

They pin their hopes on a mission from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe which wound up its work in Belgrade on Saturday after and investigation of Serbia's election fraud crisis.
Mission head Felipe Gonzalez, a former Spanish prime minister, has said he will make recommendations within a week.

The Zajedno coalition of opposition parties says it has proved to the OSCE that it was cheated of victory in Belgrade and 14 other towns in local elections -- the spark for huge street demonstrations against Milosevic over the past 35 days.
Opposition sources said the OSCE persuaded Milosevic to surrender the towns, including Belgrade but it remained unclear whether the president would effectively admit defeat.

The United States, denying Belgrade access to foreign capital until it improves it human rights record, has warned Milosevic he could face fresh sanctions. Its representative in OSCE mission said the evidence of election fraud "seems to be impressive."

Zajedno leader Vojin Dimitrijevic said "contrary to prior arrangement, President Milosevic declined to receive Gonzalez at the end of the visit, indicating that the authorities do not like the line the mission is pursuing."
In a move diplomats fear may lead to violence, the Socialists have started mounting their own counter-demonstrations. The turnouts, however have been poor.
In the southern Serbian town of Smederevo, they managed to assemble 1,500 people but the police arrested three Zajedno supporters who jeered and reportedly beat up two of them.
Zajedno said the socialists were planning to hold "final" demonstrations in Belgrade in support of Milosevic on Tuesday.
Diplomats said it would be a violation of Milosevic's promise to visiting Italian Foreign Minister Alberto Dini that he would prevent his supporters from coming to the capital.

"Do not be angry at those poor people chain-ganged for the event. They too will soon realise they have been robbed of their money and dignity by the dictator," Vesna Pesic, another Zajedno leader referring to Milosevic, told the Belgrade rally.

But a threatened blockade of all major roads as of Monday by Serbian farmers demanding the government pay back its dues for the summer crop and cut taxes, could hamper SPS plans to bus people into Belgrade by the thousands.
Diplomats fear mounting hatred and the proximity of the two rival groups could easily spark violence both Zajedno leaders and Milosevic have promised to avoid.
In another development, Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic said Serbia's central government has cut municipal budget funding to cities and towns where opposition forces recently won.

"This is a crime to punish the citizens who voted for the opposition. It's an assault on the elementary civic right -- freedom of choice...this regime has lost its head, its compass, and is behaving like an elephant in a glass shop."
